parse.title: Isometric video game graphics
parse.wikitext:
{{Redirect|Isometric graphics|isometric projection in general|Isometric projection}}
{{short description|Type of video game graphics}}
[[File:Pac-Mania gameplay.png|thumb|''[[Pac-Mania]]'', a spin-off of ''[[Pac-Man]]'' that uses isometric graphics]]
{{VG Graphics}}

'''Isometric video game graphics''' are visuals employed in [[video games]] and [[digital art]] that produce a [[Three-dimensional space|three-dimensional (3D) effect]] through [[parallel projection]]; which angles the [[Camera angle|viewpoint]] to reveal facets of the environment that would otherwise not be visible from a [[top-down perspective]] or [[Side-scrolling video game|side view]]. Despite the name, isometric computer graphics are rarely truly [[Isometric projection|isometric]];{{or|date=August 2026}} i.e., the {{math|x}}, {{math|y}}, and {{math|z}} axes are not necessarily oriented 120° to each other. Instead, a variety of angles are used, with [[dimetric projection]] or a 2:1 pixel ratio being the most common.{{or|date=August 2026}} The terms "isometric 3D", "3/4 perspective", "3/4 view", "[[2.5D]]", and "pseudo 3D" are also sometimes used, although these terms can bear slightly different meanings in other contexts.

Once common, isometric projection became less so with the advent of more powerful [[3D computer graphics|3D graphics]] systems, and as video games began to focus more on action and individual characters.<ref name="usgamer"/> However, video games using isometric projection—especially [[computer role-playing game]]s—saw a resurgence in the 2010s within the [[Indie game|indie gaming]] scene.<ref name="usgamer">{{cite web | url = http://www.usgamer.net/articles/twisted-perspective-the-continued-relevance-of-isometric-games | title = Retronauts: The Continued Relevance of Isometric Games | last = Signor | first = Jeremy | date = 2014-12-19 | website = usgamer.net | publisher = Gamer Network | access-date = 2017-04-01 | archive-date = 2015-08-09 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150809052629/http://www.usgamer.net/articles/twisted-perspective-the-continued-relevance-of-isometric-games | url-status = dead }}</ref><ref name="bestlooking">
{{cite web
 | url = https://kotaku.com/the-best-looking-isometric-games-5991061
 | title = The Best-Looking Isometric Games
 | last = Vas | first = Gergo | date = 2013-03-18
 | website = kotaku.com | publisher = Gizmodo Media Group

}}
</ref>

== Overview ==
===Advantages===

{{quote box|width=35%|1=A well-executed isometric system should never have the player thinking about the camera. You should be able to quickly and intuitively move the view to what you need to look at and never consider the camera mechanics. Trying to run a full-3D camera while playing out a real-time tactical battle is certain to cause a [[helmet fire]] in new players as they are quickly overwhelmed by the mechanics. |2=Trent Oster, co-founder of [[BioWare]] and founder of [[Beamdog]]<ref name="usgamer"/>}}

In [[video game development]] and [[pixel art]], the technique has become popular because of the ease with which [[2D computer graphics|2D]] [[Sprite (computer graphics)|sprite]]- and [[tile-based video game|tile-based]] graphics can be made to represent [[3D computer graphics|3D]] gaming environments. Because [[parallel projection|parallel projected]] objects do not change in size as they move about an area, there is no need for the computer to scale [[Sprite (computer graphics)|sprites]] or do the complex calculations necessary to simulate [[perspective (visual)|visual perspective]]. This allowed [[History of video game consoles (third generation)|8-bit]] and [[History of video game consoles (fourth generation)|16-bit]] game systems (and, more recently, [[handheld game console|handheld]] and [[mobile phone|mobile]] systems) to portray large game areas quickly and easily. And, while the [[impossible object|depth confusion problems]] of parallel projection can sometimes be a problem, good game and level design can alleviate this.

Though not limited strictly to isometric video game graphics, [[Pre-rendering|pre-rendered]] 2D graphics can possess a higher fidelity and use more advanced graphical techniques than may be possible on commonly available computer hardware, even with [[hardware acceleration|3D hardware acceleration]].<ref name="prerend">{{cite web | url =https://kotaku.com/video-games-with-the-most-memorable-pre-rendered-backgr-499808427 | title =Video Games With The Most Memorable Pre-Rendered Backgrounds | last =Vas | first =Gergo | date =2013-05-10 | website =Kotaku.com | publisher =Gizmodo Media Group | access-date =2017-04-01}}</ref> Similarly to modern [[Computer-generated imagery|CGI]] used in [[motion picture]]s, graphics can be rendered once on a powerful [[super computer]] or [[render farm]], and then displayed many times on less powerful consumer hardware, such as on [[television set]]s, [[tablet computers]] and [[smartphone]]s. This means that static pre-rendered isometric graphics often look better compared to their contemporary real-time-rendered counterparts, and may age better over time compared to their peers.<ref name="bestlooking"/> However, this advantage may be less pronounced today than it was in the past, as developments in graphical technology equalize or produce [[diminishing returns]], and current levels of graphical fidelity become "good enough" for many people.{{citation needed|date=May 2021}}

There are also gameplay advantages to using an isometric or near-isometric perspective in video games. For instance, compared to a purely [[Top-down perspective|top-down]] game, they add a third dimension, opening up new avenues for aiming and [[Platform game|platforming]].<ref name="usgamer"/> Compared to a [[First-person (video games)|first-]] or [[Third-person shooter|third-person]] video game, they allow a player to more easily field and control a large number of units, such as a full [[Party (role-playing games)|party of characters]] in a [[computer role-playing game]], or an army of minions in a [[real-time strategy video game|real-time strategy game]].<ref name="usgamer"/> Further, they may alleviate situations where a player may become distracted from a game's core [[Game mechanics|mechanics]] by having to constantly manage an unwieldy 3D camera.<ref name="usgamer"/> I.e., the player can focus on playing the game itself, and not on manipulating the game's camera.<ref name="usgamer"/>

In the present day, rather than being purely a source of nostalgia, the revival of isometric projection is the result of tangible design benefits.<ref name="usgamer"/>

===Disadvantages===
Some disadvantages of pre-rendered isometric graphics are that, as [[display resolution]]s and [[display aspect ratio]]s continue to evolve, static 2D images need to be re-rendered each time in order to keep pace, or potentially suffer from the effects of [[pixelation]] and require [[anti-aliasing]]. Re-rendering a game's graphics is not always possible, however; as was the case in 2012, when [[Beamdog]] [[Video game remake|remade]] BioWare's ''[[Baldur's Gate (video game)|Baldur's Gate]]'' (1998). Beamdog were lacking the original developers' creative art assets (the original data was lost in a flood<ref name="kotakusprites">{{cite web | url =https://kotaku.com/the-struggle-to-bring-back-baldur-s-gate-after-17-years-1768303595 | title =The Struggle To Bring Back Baldur's Gate After 17 Years | last =Grayson | first =Nathan | date =2016-04-01 | website =Kotaku.com | publisher =Gizmodo Media Group | access-date =2017-04-11 | quote = It was a big challenge because all of the Baldur's Gate original assets like the 3D models that make up these sprites, the 3D models for the levels in the original game, these archives were lost.}}</ref>) and opted for simple [[2D computer graphics#Scaling|2D graphics scaling]] with "smoothing", without re-rendering the game's sprites. The results were a certain "fuzziness", or lack of "crispness", compared to the original game's graphics.{{citation needed|date=May 2021}} This does not affect real-time rendered polygonal isometric video games, however, as changing their display resolutions or aspect ratios is trivial, in comparison.

===Differences from "true" isometric projection===
{{Unreferenced section|date=March 2025}}
[[File:Comparison of graphical projections.svg|thumb|Comparison of common graphical projections]]
The projection commonly used in video games deviates slightly from "true" isometric due to the limitations of [[raster graphics]]. Lines in the {{math|x}} and {{math|y}} directions would not follow a neat pixel pattern if drawn in the required 30° to the horizontal. While modern computers can eliminate this problem using [[Spatial anti-aliasing|anti-aliasing]], earlier computer graphics did not support enough colors or possess enough CPU power to accomplish this. Instead, a 2:1 pixel pattern ratio would be used to draw the {{math|x}} and {{math|y}} axis lines, resulting in these axes following a ≈26.565° ({{math|arctan(1/2)}}) angle to the horizontal. (Game systems that do not use [[pixel|square pixels]] could, however, yield different angles, including "true" isometric.) Therefore, this form of projection is more accurately described as a variation of [[dimetric projection]], since only two of the three angles between the axes are equal to each other, i.e., {{math|(≈116.565°, ≈116.565°, ≈126.870°)}}.

== History ==

Some [[3D computer graphics|three-dimensional]] games were released as early as the 1970s, but the first video games to use the distinct visual style of isometric projection in the meaning described above were [[arcade games]] in the early 1980s.

=== 1980s ===

The use of isometric graphics in video games began with [[Data East]]'s arcade game ''[[Treasure Island (1981 video game)|Treasure Island]]'',<ref>{{KLOV game|id=10187|name=Treasure Island}}</ref> released in Japan in September 1981,<ref>{{cite web |title=Treasure Island (Registration Number PA0000187784) |url=https://cocatalog.loc.gov |website=[[United States Copyright Office]] |access-date=5 May 2021}}</ref> but it was not released internationally until June 1982.<ref name="Akagi">{{cite book |last1=Akagi |first1=Masumi |title=アーケードTVゲームリスト国内•海外編(1971-2005) |trans-title=Arcade TV Game List: Domestic • Overseas Edition (1971-2005) |date=October 13, 2006 |publisher=Amusement News Agency |language=ja |location=Japan |isbn=978-4990251215 |pages=35, 115, 131 |url=https://archive.org/details/ArcadeGameList1971-2005/page/n36}}</ref> The first isometric game to be released internationally was [[Sega]]'s ''[[Zaxxon]]'', which was significantly more popular and influential;<ref name=Perron>{{cite book |last1=Perron |first1=Bernard |last2=Wolf |first2=Mark J. P. |title=The Video Game Theory Reader 2 |date=12 November 2008 |publisher=Taylor & Francis |isbn=978-0-415-96282-7 |page=158 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oe0zNalKkTgC&pg=PA158 |access-date=13 November 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{KLOV game|id=12757|name=Zaxxon}}</ref> it was released in Japan in December 1981<ref name="US">{{cite web |title=Zaxxon (Registration Number PA0000135301) |url=https://cocatalog.loc.gov |website=United States Copyright Office |access-date=5 May 2021}}</ref> and internationally in April 1982.<ref name="Akagi"/> ''Zaxxon'' is an [[isometric shooter]] where the player flies a space plane through [[scrolling]] levels. It is also one of the first video games to display shadows.<ref name=Perron/>

Another early isometric game is ''[[Q*bert]]''.<ref>{{KLOV game|id=9182|name=Q*bert}}</ref> [[Warren Davis (actor)|Warren Davis]] and Jeff Lee began programming the concept around April 1982. The game's production began in the summer and then released in October or November 1982.<ref>{{cite web|last=Davis|first=Warren|title=The Creation of Q*Bert|url=http://www.coinop.org/features/qbstory.aspx|work=Coinop.org|access-date=26 September 2011|author-link=Warren Davis (actor)}}</ref> ''Q*bert'' shows a static pyramid in an isometric perspective, with the player controlling a character which can jump around on the pyramid.<ref name=Perron/>

In February 1983,<ref name="Akagi"/> the [[isometric platform game|isometric platform]] arcade game ''[[Congo Bongo]]'' was released, running on the same hardware as ''Zaxxon''.<ref>{{KLOV game|id=7384|name=Congo Bongo}}</ref> It allows the player character to traverse non-scrolling isometric levels, including three-dimensional climbing and falling. The same is possible in the arcade title ''[[Marble Madness]]'', released in 1984.

{{multiple image
| width             = 150
| image1            = Sprite anatomy 2d.svg
| image2            = Sprite anatomy 3d.svg
| footer            = 2D (at left) and 3D (at right) coordinates of a typical dimetric video game sprite
}}

In 1983, isometric games were no longer exclusive to the arcade market and also entered home computers, with the release of ''[[Blue Max (video game)|Blue Max]]'' for the [[Atari 8-bit computers]] and ''[[Ant Attack]]'' for the [[ZX Spectrum]]. In ''Ant Attack'', the player can move forward in any direction of the scrolling game, offering complete free movement rather than fixed to one axis as with ''Zaxxon''. The views can also be changed around a [[Cardinal direction|90 degrees axis]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Sculptin the new shape of Spectrum games|url=http://www.worldofspectrum.org/showmag.cgi?mag=SinclairUser/Issue021/Pages/SinclairUser02100088.jpg|journal=[[Sinclair User]]|date=December 1983|issue=21|access-date=2009-03-02}}</ref> The ZX Spectrum magazine, ''[[Crash (magazine)|Crash]]'', consequently awarded it 100% in the graphics category for this new technique, known as "Soft Solid 3-D".<ref>{{cite journal|title=Soft Solid 3D Ant Attack|url=http://www.crashonline.org.uk/01/antattack.htm|journal=[[Crash (magazine)|CRASH]]|date=February 1984|issue=1|access-date=2008-09-29}}</ref>

A year later, the ZX Spectrum game ''[[Knight Lore]]'' was released. It was generally regarded as a revolutionary title<ref name="GamesTM">{{cite book |title=Retro Micro Games Action – The Best of gamesTM Retro Volume 1 |year=2006 |publisher=Highbury Entertainment |chapter=Ultimate Play the Game – Company Lookback |page=25}}</ref> that defined the subsequent genre of isometric adventure games.<ref name="SIGGRAPH">{{cite web | url=http://www.siggraph.org/publications/newsletter/v32n2/contributions/collins.html | title=Game Graphics During the 8-bit Computer Era | author=Steven Collins | publisher=SIGGRAPH | work=Computer Graphics Newsletters | access-date=2007-08-16 | archive-url=https://archive.today/20120909170003/http://www.siggraph.org/publications/newsletter/v32n2/contributions/collins.html | archive-date=2012-09-09 | url-status=dead }}</ref> Following ''Knight Lore'', many isometric titles were seen on home computers – to an extent that it once was regarded as being the second most cloned piece of software after ''[[WordStar]]'', according to researcher Jan Krikke.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Axonometry: a matter of perspective |date=July–August 2000|last=Krikke |first=J.|journal=IEEE Computer Graphics and Applications |volume=20|issue=4|pages=7–11|doi=10.1109/38.851742 |bibcode=2000ICGA...20d...7K }} "''Knight Lore'' was said to be the second most cloned piece of software after the word- processing program ''Word Star''."</ref> Other examples out of those were ''[[Highway Encounter]]'' (1985), ''[[Batman (1986 video game)|Batman]]'' (1986), ''[[Head Over Heels (video game)|Head Over Heels]]'' (1987)<ref>{{cite journal|title=Looking for an old angle|url=http://www.crashonline.org.uk/51/runagain.htm|journal=[[Crash (magazine)|CRASH]]|date=April 1988|issue=51|access-date=2008-09-29}}</ref> and ''[[La Abadía del Crimen]]'' (1987).

Isometric perspective was not limited to action and adventure games. For example, the 1989 strategy game ''[[Populous (video game)|Populous]]'' uses isometric perspective.

=== 1990s ===
{{multiple image
| image1            = Pixelart-tv-iso-2.png
| width1            = 150
| height1           = 150
| alt1              = Pixel art
| caption1          = A television set drawn in near-isometric 2:1 [[pixel art]] (enlarged to show the pixel structure)<ref>Note: The 2:1 pixel pattern in the near-isometric image allows smoother lines than in the isometric one.</ref>
| image2            = Fallout camera angles.png
| width2            = 150
| height2           = 150
| alt2              = Rendering of a scene emulating Fallout 2's perspective
| caption2          = [[3D rendering]] mimicking the video game ''[[Fallout (video game)|Fallout]]'''s use of [[trimetric projection]] and a [[Hex map|hexagonal grid]]
}}

Throughout the 1990s, a number of successful computer games used a fixed isometric perspective, such as ''[[A-Train III]]'' (1990), ''[[Syndicate (1993 video game)|Syndicate]]'' (1993), ''[[SimCity 2000]]'' (1994), ''[[Civilization II]]'' (1996), ''[[X-COM]]'' (1994), and ''[[Diablo (video game)|Diablo]]'' (1996). But with the advent of [[3D acceleration]] on personal computers and gaming consoles, games previously using a 2D perspective generally started switching to true 3D (and [[perspective projection]]) instead. This can be seen in the successors to the above games: for instance ''[[SimCity (2013 video game)|SimCity]]'' (2013), ''[[Civilization VI]]'' (2016), ''[[XCOM: Enemy Unknown]]'' (2012) and ''[[Diablo III]]'' (2012) all use 3D polygonal graphics; and while ''[[Diablo II]]'' (2000) used fixed-perspective 2D perspective like its predecessor, it optionally allowed for perspective scaling of the sprites in the distance to lend it a "pseudo-3D" appearance.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_pwwi/is_200005/ai_mark15009744 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070309033612/http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_pwwi/is_200005/ai_mark15009744 |url-status=usurped |archive-date=March 9, 2007 |title=Diablo II Nears Completion As Blizzard Prepares For Final Phase Of Beta Testing |agency=[[Marketwire]] |date=May 2000 |work=Market Wire |access-date=2008-09-29 }}</ref>

Also during the 1990s, isometric graphics began being used for Japanese [[role-playing video game]]s (JRPGs) on [[video game console|console systems]], particularly [[tactical role-playing game]]s, many of which still use isometric graphics today. Examples include ''[[Front Mission]]'' (1995), ''[[Tactics Ogre]]'' (1995) and ''[[Final Fantasy Tactics]]'' (1997)—the latter of which used [[3D computer graphics|3D graphics]] to create an environment where the player could freely rotate the camera. Other titles such as ''[[Vandal Hearts]]'' (1996) and ''[[Breath of Fire III]]'' (1997) carefully emulated an isometric or parallel view, but actually used perspective projection.

Isometric, or similar, perspectives become popular in [[role-playing video games]], such as ''[[Fallout (video game)|Fallout]]'' and ''[[Baldur's Gate]]''.  In some cases, these role-playing games became defined by their isometric perspective, which allows larger scale battles.<ref name="usgamer"/>

===2010s===
Isometric projection has seen continued relevance in the new millennium with the release of several newly-[[crowdfunded]] role-playing games on [[Kickstarter]].<ref name="usgamer"/> These include the ''[[Shadowrun Returns]]'' series (2013–2015) by [[Harebrained Schemes]]; the ''[[Pillars of Eternity]]'' series (2015–2018) and ''[[Tyranny (video game)|Tyranny]]'' (2016) by [[Obsidian Entertainment]]; and ''[[Torment: Tides of Numenera]]'' (2017) by [[inXile Entertainment]].{{fact|date=April 2023}} Both Obsidian Entertainment and inXile Entertainment have employed, or were founded by, former members of Black Isle Studios and Interplay Entertainment. Obsidian Entertainment in particular wanted to "bring back the look and feel of the [[Infinity Engine]] games like ''Baldur's Gate'', ''[[Icewind Dale]]'', and ''[[Planescape: Torment]]''".<ref name="usgamer"/> Lastly, several pseudo-isometric 3D RPGs, such as ''[[Divinity: Original Sin]]'' (2014), ''[[Wasteland 2]]'' (2014) and ''[[Dead State]]'' (2014), have been crowdfunded using Kickstarter. These titles differ from the above games, however, in that they use ''perspective projection'' instead of ''parallel projection''.{{fact|date=April 2023}}

===Use of related projections and techniques===
[[File:Graphical projection comparison.png|thumb|right|Comparison of several types of [[graphical projection]]. Among 3/4 views, the presence of one or more 90° principal angles is often a good indicator that the perspective used is ''[[oblique projection]]''.]]
The term "isometric perspective" is frequently misapplied to any game with an angled, overhead view. These include the aforementioned [[dimetric projection|dimetrically projected]] video games; games that use [[trimetric projection]], such as ''[[Fallout (computer game)|Fallout]]'' (1997)<ref name=gspot_fo>{{cite web | last = Green | first = Jeff | title = GameSpot Preview: Arcanum | work = [[GameSpot]] | publisher = [[CNET Networks|CNET Networks, Inc]] | date = 2000-02-29 | url = http://www.gamespot.com/features/arcanum_pre/ | access-date = 2008-01-10}}</ref> and ''[[SimCity 4]]'' (2003);<ref name=ign_sc4>{{cite web | last = Butts | first = Steve | title = SimCity 4: Rush Hour Preview |work=IGN PC |publisher =[[IGN|IGN Entertainment, Inc]] | date =2003-09-09 | url = http://pc.ign.com/articles/437/437280p1.html | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20030920051234/http://pc.ign.com/articles/437/437280p1.html | url-status = dead | archive-date = September 20, 2003 | access-date = 2008-01-10}}</ref> games that use [[oblique projection]], such as ''[[Ultima Online]]'' (1997)<ref name=gamasutra_uol>{{cite web | last =Greely | first =Dave  |author2=Ben Sawyer | title =Has Origin Created the First True Online Game World? | work =[[Gamasutra]] | publisher =CMP Media LLC| date =1997-08-19 | url =https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/has-origin-created-the-first-true-online-game-world- | access-date =2007-12-17  }}</ref> and ''[[Divine Divinity]]'' (2002);<ref>{{cite web | url =https://www.gamespot.com/articles/divine-divinity-goes-gold/1100-2874202/ | title =Divine Divinity goes gold | last =Walker | first =Trey | date =2002-07-12 | website =GameSpot | publisher =CBS Interactive | access-date =2017-04-11}}</ref> and games that use a combination of [[perspective projection]] and a [[bird's eye view]], such as ''[[Silent Storm]]'' (2003),<ref name=cvg_ss>{{cite web | last =O'Hagan | first =Steve | title =PC Previews: Silent Storm | work =[[ComputerAndVideoGames.com]] |publisher=[[Future Publishing|Future Publishing Limited]] | date =2008-08-07 | url =http://www.computerandvideogames.com/article.php?id=94816 | access-date =2007-12-13  }}</ref> ''[[Torchlight]]'' (2009)<ref name=tlight_gr>{{cite web | last = McDougall | first = Jaz | title = Torchlight Review | publisher = [[Games Radar]] | date = November 4, 2009 | url = http://www.gamesradar.com/pc/torchlight/review/torchlight/a-20091104113625828034/g-2009100517263770009 | access-date = 2009-11-06 | archive-date = 2015-10-13 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20151013175227/http://www.gamesradar.com/torchlight/ | url-status = dead }}</ref> and ''[[Divinity: Original Sin]]'' (2014).<ref>{{cite web | url =https://kotaku.com/im-glad-theyre-still-making-games-like-divinity-origin-1600013660 | title =I'm Glad They're Still Making Games Like Divinity: Original Sin | last =Hamilton | first =Kirk | date =2014-07-03 | website =Kotaku | publisher =Gizmodo Media Group | access-date =2017-04-11}}</ref>

Also, not all "isometric" video games rely solely on pre-rendered 2D sprites. There are, for instance, titles which use polygonal 3D graphics completely, but render their graphics using parallel projection instead of perspective projection, such as ''[[Syndicate Wars]]'' (1996), ''[[Dungeon Keeper]]'' (1997) and ''[[Depths of Peril]]'' (2007); games which use a combination of pre-rendered 2D backgrounds and real-time rendered 3D character models, such as ''[[The Temple of Elemental Evil (video game)|The Temple of Elemental Evil]]'' (2003) and ''[[Torment: Tides of Numenera]]'' (2017); and games which combine real-time rendered 3D backgrounds with hand-drawn 2D character sprites, such as ''[[Final Fantasy Tactics]]'' (1997) and ''[[Disgaea: Hour of Darkness]]'' (2003).

One advantage of top-down ''oblique projection'' over other near-isometric perspectives, is that objects fit more snugly within non-overlapping square graphical tiles, thereby potentially eliminating the need for an additional [[Z-order]] in calculations, and requiring fewer pixels.

== Mapping screen to world coordinates ==
{{Unreferenced section|date=December 2024}}

[[File:Findtilecoordinates.png|left|thumb|Finding world coordinates]]

One of the most common problems with programming games that use isometric (or more likely dimetric) projections is the ability to map between events that happen on the 2D plane of the screen and the actual location in the isometric space, called world space. A common example is picking the tile that lies right under the cursor when a user clicks. One such method is using the same [[Rotation_matrix|rotation matrices]] that originally produced the isometric view in reverse to turn a point in screen coordinates into a point that would lie on the game board surface before it was rotated. Then, the world x and y values can be calculated by dividing by the tile width and height.

Another way that is less computationally intensive and can have good results if the method is called on every frame, rests on the assumption that a square board was rotated by 45 degrees and then squashed to be half its original height. A virtual grid is overlaid on the projection as shown on the diagram, with axes virtual-x and virtual-y. Clicking any tile on the central axis of the board where (x, y) = (tileMapWidth / 2, y), will produce the same tile value for both world-x and world-y which in this example is 3 (0 indexed). Selecting the tile that lies one position on the right on the virtual grid, actually moves one tile less on the world-y and one tile more on the world-x. This is the formula that calculates world-x by taking the virtual-y and adding the virtual-x from the center of the board. Likewise world-y is calculated by taking virtual-y and subtracting virtual-x. These calculations measure from the central axis, as shown, so the results must be translated by half the board. For example, in the [[C (programming language)|C]] programming language:

<syntaxhighlight lang="c">
float virtualTileX = screenx / virtualTileWidth;
float virtualTileY = screeny / virtualTileHeight;

// some display systems have their origin at the bottom left while the tile map at the top left, so we need to reverse y
float inverseTileY = numberOfTilesInY - virtualTileY;

float isoTileX = inverseTileY + (virtualTileX - numberOfTilesInX / 2);
float isoTileY = inverseTileY - (virtualTileX - numberOfTilesInY / 2);
</syntaxhighlight>

This method might seem counter intuitive at first since the coordinates of a virtual grid are taken, rather than the original isometric world, and there is no one-to-one correspondence between virtual tiles and isometric tiles. A tile on the grid will contain more than one isometric tile, and depending on where it is clicked it should map to different coordinates. The key in this method is that the virtual coordinates are floating point numbers rather than integers. A virtual-x and y value can be (3.5, 3.5) which means the center of the third tile. In the diagram on the left, this falls in the third tile on the y in detail. When the virtual-x and y must add up to 4, the world x will also be 4.

== Examples ==
